title: Cooking — and the two faces of every verb
goal: Talk about food and cooking — and get to grips with aspect (*vid*): the fact that almost every Slovenian verb comes in a pair, one for an action in progress and one for an action that gets finished.
bekal: recognizing the pairs *kuhati / skuhati*, *brati / prebrati*, *jesti / pojesti*
knowing that a completed verb in the present tense actually means the future
naming ingredients, kitchen words and typical Slovenian dishes

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kuham in skuham
dialogs.intro: The dorm kitchen. Budi is cooking; Maja sits at the table and asks about one letter that changes everything.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kuham juho. Skuham jo v pol ure.
lines.id: I'm making soup. It'll be ready in half an hour.
lines.literal: I-cook soup-acc. I-will-finish-cooking it-acc in half of-hour.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Kuham in skuham — kakšna je razlika?
lines.literal: I-cook and I-finish-cooking — what-kind is difference?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kuham je zdaj. Skuham je do konca.
lines.id: "Kuham" is now. "Skuham" is all the way to the end.
lines.literal: I-cook is now. I-finish-cooking is to of-end.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Almost. It means it'll definitely get done.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: And what are you going to cook tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: Excellent. I'll eat every bit of that.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: "Pojedla" — so all of it, to the end.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Tako je. Za to imamo en glagol.
lines.id: That's right. We have one verb for that.
lines.literal: so is. for that we-have one verb.

notes: **Almost every Slovenian verb has a twin.** One for an action that is **ongoing or repeated** (imperfective, *nedovršni*), one for an action **carried through to the end** (perfective, *dovršni*). *Kuham juho* = I'm cooking soup. *Skuham juho* = I'll get the soup done.

**A completed verb in the present tense means the future.** This is the most confusing part at first: *Skuham* looks like a present tense, but it can't mean "now" — something finished can't be in progress. So it automatically jumps to the future. Slovenian gets a free future tense out of this way of thinking.

**English actually does something similar, just more loosely.** "I'm eating" versus "I'll eat it up"; "I'm reading" versus "I'll finish reading"; "I'm writing" versus "I'll write it up". The difference is that English lets you ignore the distinction, while Slovenian makes you choose before you open your mouth.

**The prefix that makes a verb perfective varies from word to word.** *s-* in *skuhati*, *pre-* in *prebrati*, *po-* in *pojesti*, *na-* in *napisati*. No rule predicts it, so learn the pairs side by side — just as you learn a noun's gender together with it.

**Bom pojedla — the full future form.** For unfinished actions, Slovenian uses *bom* + the *-l* form: *bom kuhala* (I'll be cooking). For finished ones, either works: *bom pojedla* or just *pojem*. The whole system is covered in unit 17.

grammars.title: Vid — two faces of one action
body: This table holds the pairs used most at A1. The left column is for actions in progress or repeated; the right column is for actions completed once and for all.
after: The test that never fails: ask **whether the action has a clear endpoint in this sentence**. "I read every day" — no endpoint, use *berem*. "I finished that book yesterday" — endpoint, use *sem prebral*.

In the past tense the difference is most noticeable: *Bral sem knjigo* (I was reading the book, finished or not) versus *Prebral sem knjigo* (I finished it). English often writes both as "I read the book" and adds "all the way through" when needed.

grammars.title: Prefixes that change the meaning
body: Slovenian prefixes don't only mark finished or unfinished; some of them really change the verb's meaning. The six you'll meet most:
after: Notice that the same prefix can attach to many verbs with a similar flavor: *pri-* always means approaching (*priti*, *prinesti* bring along, *priti domov* come home), and *od-* always means moving away (*oditi*, *odnesti* take away).

That's why one basic verb can produce a dozen new words. *Nesti* (carry) gives *prinesti*, *odnesti*, *ponesti*, *prenesti*, *znesti*. It's why a Slovenian dictionary looks scary even though there aren't many roots — and also why your vocabulary will grow fast once you recognize the prefixes.

blocks.text: Slovenia sits at the crossroads of four cuisines: Austrian, Italian, Hungarian and Balkan. The result is food that changes face every hundred kilometers — and food vocabulary that sometimes sounds familiar and sometimes not at all.

Dishes you'll be offered sooner or later: **kranjska klobasa** (Carniolan sausage, protected by the EU like Parma ham), **jota** (bean and sauerkraut soup), **žganci** (buckwheat mush, farmers' food), **ričet** (barley stew), **štruklji** (rolled dumplings filled with cheese or nuts), and **potica** — a walnut roll that appears at every celebration and whose recipe every family argues about.

One sentence you may need: *Ne jem svinjine* (I don't eat pork). Notice the form — *svinjina* becomes *svinjine* because the sentence is negative. Other useful ones: *Sem vegetarijanec* (male) or *Sem vegetarijanka* (female), and *Ali to vsebuje meso?* (does this have meat in it?).

blocks.text: Notice four adjectives that change with gender: **sit / sita** (full), **lačen / lačna** (hungry), **žejen / žejna** (thirsty), **utrujen / utrujena** (tired). All four are used with *sem*, not *imam* — so "I am hungry", just like English, not "I have hunger" as in French or Spanish.

blocks.title: Eating habits in Slovenia
items: **Kosilo** (lunch) is the main meal, not dinner — usually between noon and 2:00, and it almost always starts with soup.
**Malica** is a small mid-morning meal around 10:00, and at schools and workplaces it's practically an official institution.
A Slovenian host will offer you more again and again. Saying no once is considered polite, not final — so if you're really full, say *Res sem sit, hvala* with a smile.
